chunks: Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Fadhal narrated from Amr ibn Uthman from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira from Talhah ibn Zayd from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) from his father (peace be upon him) who said:

"Whoever gives a charity (sadaqah) and it is returned to him, he should not eat it, because there is no partner for Allah in anything that was designated for him; it is merely in the status of manumission (itq), so its return is not valid after it has freed [the debt/obligation]."

key_terms.الْعَتَاقَةِ: Manumission, the act of freeing a slave
key_terms.صَدَقَةٍ: Charity, voluntary alms given for the sake of God
key_terms.لَا شَرِيكَ لِلَّهِ: No partner for Allah, indicating exclusivity of the act's intent
key_terms.يُعْتِقُ: He frees, past participle of manumission

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a charity donation if it is returned to the donor?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) via a chain including Ali ibn al-Hasan ibn Faddal, emphasizing that returned charity cannot be re-consumed because the original gift was dedicated solely to Allah, mirroring the irrevocability of manumission (itq). This analogy highlights the spiritual finality of the act of giving, distinguishing it from a revocable loan or sale. The hadith underscores the principle that once a gift is given for Allah's sake, it transcends mere ownership and becomes a permanent act of worship.
